paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35), or tyrosine kinase-2 (TYK2) deficiency, is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency. Its core feature is susceptibility to mycobacterial and/or viral infections, which results from impaired cellular responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta. Patients may also have infections with other intracellular bacteria, such as Salmonella and Brucella. The first reported patient also had features of hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES), including atopic dermatitis, high serum IgE, and staphylococcal abscesses. Most patients reported later did not have these features, and impaired IL-6 responses and HIES do not appear to be intrinsic features of TYK2 deficiency (Kreins et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Minegishi et al. (2006) reported a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome. He had unusual susceptibility to a range of microorganisms, including viruses, fungi, and mycobacteria, and had atopic dermatitis with elevated serum IgE. Kreins et al. (2015) gave further details on this Japanese man (P1), who was born to consanguineous parents. He had had atopic dermatitis since 1 month of age and recurrent bacterial and viral infections since 1 year of age. He developed BCGitis at 22 months, 6 months after vaccination, and had repeated Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses, pneumonia without pneumatocele formation, otitis, and sinusitis. At 15 years of age he was admitted with sepsis after severe nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis. His viral infections included parainfluenza virus-3 pneumonia, recurrent oral HSV infections associated with tonsillitis, and molluscum contagiosum. He also had mild oral candidiasis. Laboratory studies repeatedly showed hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and high serum IgE (1,430-2,100 IU/ml). He was diagnosed with autosomal recessive HIES on the basis of an NIH score of 48 points. At 30 years of age he had ocular sarcoidosis. He had no bone fractures, and his dentition and facial appearance were normal (Kilic et al., 2012).

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, born to first-cousin parents, who received BCG vaccine at 2 months of age. Left axillary lymphadenopathy appeared at 8 months, and by 21 months he had generalized lymphadenopathy and fatigue. He had fistulous bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenitis, and M. bovis BCG was isolated from the draining cervical sinuses. At 8 years of age he developed meningitis, with Brucella spp. grown from blood and CSF. Neurobrucellosis left him with severe sensorineural hearing loss and severe cognitive impairment, and MRI showed lacunar infarcts. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve. He had no skeletal or dental features of HIES and no history of atopy, asthma, candidiasis, boils, folliculitis, or cold abscess. Serum IgE measured at 2, 11, 16, and 18 years of age was normal or slightly high (80, 115, 218, and 155 IU/ml, respectively). Kilic et al. (2012) concluded that TYK2 deficiency should be considered in patients susceptible to herpesviruses and intramacrophage pathogens, even when atopy, high serum IgE, and staphylococcal disease are absent.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) reported 7 further TYK2-deficient patients (P2-P8) from 5 unrelated families from Turkey, Morocco, Iran, and Argentina. P2 was the patient reported by Kilic et al. (2012). In a Moroccan family with first-cousin parents, a girl (P3) developed disseminated extrapulmonary tuberculosis at 13 years of age and died 15 months after symptom onset. Her brother (P4) had meningitis of unknown etiology at 8 months of age, recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels. An Iranian boy (P5) born to consanguineous parents developed BCG lymphadenitis in infancy and, at 4.5 years of age, paravertebral and psoas abscesses with pulmonary involvement. His younger sister (P6) had BCG lymphadenopathy after vaccination and was hospitalized at 1 year of age for an unknown viral infection of the skin. A 9-year-old Iranian girl (P7) born to consanguineous parents had miliary tuberculosis. An 11-year-old boy from Argentina (P8), adopted at 1 day of age, had recurrent herpes gingivostomatitis, aseptic herpes meningitis with disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions, and mild mental disability. None of P2 to P8 had documented pyogenic infections, including staphylococcal disease, or fungal infections, including mucocutaneous candidiasis, and their serum IgE levels were never high. Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype of TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infection.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy born to young nonconsanguineous parents. He received BCG vaccine on the third day of life and had repeated abscess and ulceration at the injection site. At 14 months of age he was hospitalized with BCG-associated tuberculosis of the left axillary lymph nodes. From 6 months of age he had recurrent respiratory tract infections and diarrhea. Pathogens identified during hospitalizations included Salmonella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and M. bovis BCG, and IgM antibodies to influenza A and B viruses were positive. He had no high serum IgE, atopy, staphylococcal illness, or lymphopenia. NK cells were low (3.6%) and CD19+ B cells were increased. He began to say simple words at 3 years and 4 months of age, with normal motor development, and had a small head circumference. In their review of 12 reported patients, Wu et al. (2020) found intracellular bacterial infections in 58%, recurrent viral infections in 58%, and markedly increased serum IgE in 25%. None of the 12 had the special facial features, abnormal bone development, pathologic fractures, delayed loss of deciduous teeth, or aneurysms seen in STAT3-related HIES. The review included 2 sibs reported by Nemoto, who were compound heterozygous for TYK2 mutations, had partial TYK2 deficiency with T-cell lymphopenia, and developed EBV-associated B-cell lymphoma.
